articles.title: What Running a 200-Game Browser Arcade Taught Me About Instant-Play UX
articles.excerpt: What Running a 200-Game Browser Arcade Taught Me About Instant-Play UX I help run PlayPokiGame, a free collection of a few hundred casual HTML5 games you can play right in the browser — no downloads,…
articles.body: What Running a 200-Game Browser Arcade Taught Me About Instant-Play UX I help run PlayPokiGame, a free collection of a few hundred casual HTML5 games you can play right in the browser — no downloads, no signups. After watching how real players actually use it, I've developed strong opinions about what "instant play" really requires. Here's what the data and the rage-quits taught me. 1. Your load budget is 3 seconds, not 30 The single biggest predictor of whether someone plays a game on our site isn't the rating or the thumbnail — it's time-to-interactive. Games that show a playable frame within ~3 seconds get dramatically more sessions than ones with a 10-second logo parade. On mobile networks this matters even more. We now treat every splash screen longer than a beat as a bug.
articles.author: toolswithalex

articles.title: Convert iPhone HEIC photos to JPG in the browser with JavaScript
articles.excerpt: iPhones save photos as HEIC by default. They are about half the size of JPG, but many websites, forms and Windows apps cannot open them. A common request is "let users upload an iPhone photo", and mos…
articles.body: iPhones save photos as HEIC by default. They are about half the size of JPG, but many websites, forms and Windows apps cannot open them. A common request is "let users upload an iPhone photo", and most upload forms reject .heic . You can convert HEIC to JPG entirely in the browser, with no server. Here is a small, working approach using the heic2any library. Why not just use a canvas? Normally you would draw an image onto a canvas and call toBlob() . That fails for HEIC in most browsers, because only Safari can decode HEIC natively. Chrome, Firefox and Edge cannot load a .heic file into an <img> . So you need a decoder, and heic2any ships one compiled to WebAssembly.

articles.title: Treat Your LLM Agent Like a New Bank Teller
articles.excerpt: I have spent most of my career building financial systems: a multi-tenant SACCO platform, an insurance broker portal, POS software. None of that was "AI safety." But when I started wiring LLMs into do…
articles.body: I have spent most of my career building financial systems: a multi-tenant SACCO platform, an insurance broker portal, POS software. None of that was "AI safety." But when I started wiring LLMs into document workflows, I noticed the threat model felt familiar. An LLM agent with tools is a new employee who is fast, eager, literate, and completely unable to tell a customer from a con artist. Banks have dealt with that employee for a century. The controls exist. We just forget to apply them to the model. Here are the five that carried over. 1. The teller does not set their own limits In a SACCO, a teller can post a withdrawal up to a threshold. Above it, a supervisor approves. The teller cannot change the threshold, no matter how convincing the customer is.

articles.title: ShellCheck Passed Every File. The Pipeline Was Still Broken.
articles.excerpt: ShellCheck Passed Every File. The Pipeline Was Still Broken. ShellCheck is great at what it does. So is Pylint. So is every linter you've one file at a . Here's the failure mode that keeps biting me.…
articles.body: ShellCheck Passed Every File. The Pipeline Was Still Broken. ShellCheck is great at what it does. So is Pylint. So is every linter you've ever run in CI. They all share one blind spot: they look at one file at a time . Here's the failure mode that keeps biting me. A deploy script calls ./cleanup.sh . The linter passes. The pipeline runs. And it fails — because cleanup.sh was renamed two sprints ago and nobody updated the caller. No linter on earth flags a call to a file that doesn't exist, because no linter is looking at the relationships between files . The same blind spot shows up with agents.

articles.body: In 1787, Thomas Rowlandson drew an ox loose on Westminster Bridge. Hats flying, people climbing the railings, total panic. That's roughly how it feels to drop a Rust linter into a five-year-old JavaScript project. Oxlint and Oxfmt are the linter and formatter from the Oxc project. Between them they're downloaded about 26 million times a week, and the docs make bold claims: Oxlint is "50 to 100 times faster than ESLint", and Oxfmt is "approximately 30x faster than Prettier." Bold claims deserve a stopwatch. So we picked a real, popular React codebase and timed both setups on the same laptop. But the stopwatch turned out to be the boring part. The test We used Excalidraw , the open-source whiteboard app.

articles.body: A stakeholder analysis for a software project is a short table of the people who can shape, block, use or pay for the product, with what each of them needs and how much say they have. You build it in the first days of discovery, use it to plan interviews and sign-off, and keep it up to date until handover. Why discovery starts with people Most of what a discovery phase has to find out lives in people's heads, not in documents. The sponsor knows the budget limit. articles.body: Full spoilers follow for VisionQuest Episodes 3 and 4, which are streaming now on Disney+. VisionQuest is turning out to be quite the pleasant little surprise. What initially seemed like an obligatory but unneeded follow-up to a loose end from WandaVision is rapidly developing into a series with plenty of heart, soul, and depth of its own. It never pays to count out Paul Bettany's synthetic hero. Mind you, entertaining as the first two episodes were, my one real reservation with VisionQuest out of the gate was that it was a bit difficult to connect with this version of Bettany's character. As he himself says, he has all the memories of the original Vision but none of his soul.

articles.title: Cooking Up Magick Book Review
articles.excerpt: Cooking Up Magick Book Review
articles.body: The first book in a new series called The Dell Chronicles, HL Bernabe’s Cooking Up Magick sets out to be a cozier fantasy version of The Lord of the Rings . And in many ways, it does pull directly from J.R.R. Tolkien’s world. The main character, Paisley, is a halfling who gets swept up on an adventure with a pair of dwarves, but unbeknownst to her, there’s also an evil overlord that has just returned after centuries – and she’s the only hope the world has to actually stop him. The similarities to The Hobbit and LOTR pretty much end there though, and you don’t get nearly enough detail in the first book to effectively flesh out this alternate version of Middle-earth. What you do get is a lovable main character who is surrounded by an interesting cast of characters.
